A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Video Panels for Long Video Understanding. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite extensive layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original paneling evaluations across five benchmarks, fine-tuning experiments, ablations, and qualitative examples.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds commercial-model evaluations, question-type analyses, and temporal-encoding experiments.

M1.justification: Supplementary Section 8 introduces optional panels-F and panels-T variants that overlay frame indices or timestamps. These alter the visual inputs. The default dynamic sampling, panel construction, and fine-tuning objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use VideoMME, TimeScope, MLVU, MF2, and VNBench, with LLaVA-Video-178K for fine-tuning. The new question-type breakdowns and qualitative examples concern retained benchmark coverage; commercial models do not introduce new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds baseline-versus-panel comparisons for models labeled GPT-4o-mini-2025-04-14 and GPT-4.1-2025-04-14 on VideoMME. Existing open-model comparators and the low-res pooling baseline are retained. The cited Qwen2.5 default result was already discussed in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds commercial-model evaluation configurations using 8 and 32 input frames and a controlled comparison of unencoded, frame-index, and timestamp panels with 32-frame Qwen2.5 on MLVU. Retained experiments preserve their stated metrics, sampling defaults, context sizes, and fine-tuning budget.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends diagnostic analysis through an MLVU question-type breakdown, targeted temporal-encoding ablations, reported overfitting when fine-tuning pooled representations, and two additional qualitative cases. These investigate failure conditions and possible remedies beyond the retained duration, context-size, panel-grid, threshold, and prompt ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates for its experimental results.

E6.justification: New result families extend evidence to commercial models and ordering failures. Added Table 1 rows report baseline/paneled VideoMME accuracies of 51.1/53.6 and 72.5/73.6. New Tables 5–6 report question-type outcomes and ordering accuracy of 48.6 without explicit encoding versus 50.6 with either encoding variant. Retained Tables 1–4 and the relocated prompt table preserve their numerical results.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 corrects the panel-construction condition from gamma C >= D to gamma C < D, resolving its contradiction with the unchanged sampling rule in Equation 1. The remaining mathematical formulation and training objective are retained; no proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the claims of training-free, parameter-free, model-agnostic paneling, broad benchmark improvements, and further gains through fine-tuning. Additional commercial-model evidence supports these existing claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies missing temporal encoding as a limitation affecting ordering questions and explains the task-dependent tradeoffs of index and timestamp overlays. It also expands discussion of native long-video models. The central spatial-versus-temporal tradeoff interpretation remains.

D1.justification: v1 promises code upon acceptance; v2 states that code is available and supplies a project link. v2 also identifies Leonardo at CINECA as a computing resource. Conversely, some dataset counts, including TimeScope's 1500/450-video counts, disappear. Core implementation and fine-tuning settings remain documented.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including GPT-4, MovieChat, SlowFast-LLaVA, Visual Context Window Extension, and An Image Grid Can Be Worth a Video. Related work more explicitly distinguishes frame-level from token-level processing and contrasts its video-model and fine-tuning contributions with earlier composite-image approaches.

P1.justification: v2 edits paragraphs and captions, retitles experimental subsections, condenses the main dataset description, and organizes supplementary content into numbered sections. The dedicated reproducibility statement is removed and acknowledgments are added. Much of the original narrative and section sequence remains.

P2.justification: The document changes from one-column to two-column formatting throughout. Figures 3–4 switch from side-by-side to vertically stacked plots, and tables and illustrations are resized and relocated. Table 1 gains a commercial-model block; two tables and two qualitative figures are added. The original prompt table becomes Table 7.

improvement.justification: The added failure analysis and temporal-encoding experiments clarify applicability limits, while commercial-model comparisons, the corrected paneling condition, and reported code access strengthen the paper. These gains are tempered by an unexplained inconsistency: v2 reports plain-panel MLVU accuracy as 64.9 in Table 1 but 63.4 in Table 6 under the same stated model and frame count. Overall, the evidence supports a limited quality improvement.
